title: You thought the story of Lazarus was only about a dead man walking out of a tomb.
paragraphs: You thought the story of Lazarus was only about a dead man walking out of a tomb.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Lazarus was not the center of the story.
Death was.
And Jesus walked straight into it on purpose.

The raising of Lazarus in John 11 is not merely a miracle narrative. It is a public confrontation between the Author of Life and the kingdom of death itself. It is one of the deepest revelations of Christ’s identity ever recorded in Scripture, and hidden inside the original language are details most readers never notice.
The story begins in tension, not triumph.
“Now a certain man was sick, Lazarus of Bethany…” — John 11:1
The Greek text says:

“Ἦν δέ τις ἀσθενῶν, Λάζαρος…”
“Ēn de tis asthenōn, Lazaros…”
The word “ἀσθενῶν” (asthenōn) means weak, powerless, without strength. This was not a minor illness. Lazarus was fading.
And Jesus knew it.
That changes everything.
Because when the message reached Jesus, Scripture says:
“Lord, behold, he whom You love is sick.” — John 11:3
The Greek word for love here is not “agapē.”
It is:
“φιλεῖς” (phileis)
A deeply personal affection. Brotherly love. Intimate friendship.
This was not a distant follower.
Lazarus was loved personally by Jesus.
And still…
Jesus waited.
“Then after He said to the disciples, ‘Let us go to Judea again.’” — John 11:7
He delayed two full days.
That delay confuses people even now. Why would Jesus wait while someone He loved suffered and died?
Because Christ was never reacting to death.
He was orchestrating a revelation.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
Most readers miss the prophetic timing hidden in Jewish burial culture.
In first-century Judaism, many believed the spirit hovered near the body for three days, hoping to return. By the fourth day, decomposition made restoration humanly impossible.
And Lazarus had been dead four days.
Not one.
Not two.
Not three.
Four.
Jesus intentionally arrived after every human hope had expired.
God saw it.
The impossible was the point.
When Martha meets Jesus, she says:
“Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” — John 11:21
That sentence is loaded with grief and theology.
She believed Jesus could prevent death.
But she did not yet understand He could reverse it.
Then comes one of the most explosive declarations in all Scripture.
Jesus says:
“I am the resurrection and the life.” — John 11:25
In Greek:

“ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή”
“Egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē.”
“ἐγώ εἰμι” (Egō eimi) means “I AM.”
This was not accidental language.
Jesus was invoking the divine name revealed in Exodus.
When Moses asked God His name, the Hebrew text says:

“אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה”
“Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh”
“I AM THAT I AM.” — Exodus 3:14
Jesus was not merely claiming power from God.
He was revealing Himself as God in flesh.
Read that again.
“I AM the resurrection.”
Not “I bring resurrection.”
Not “I teach resurrection.”
He IS resurrection itself.
Life is not something Jesus possesses externally.
Life proceeds from His very being.
That is why death panics in His presence.
And then comes the shortest verse in English Scripture:
“Jesus wept.” — John 11:35
In Greek:

“ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς”
“Edakrysen ho Iēsous.”
But the original meaning carries more weight than modern readers realize.
This word for weeping is not uncontrolled mourning.
It describes tears flowing silently.
Measured grief.
Divine sorrow.
Why would Jesus cry when He already knew Lazarus was about to rise?
Because death was never part of God’s original creation.
Every funeral screams the consequences of sin.
Romans 5:12 says:
“Through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin.”
Death is an intruder.
A curse.
And Jesus stood before the tomb furious at what sin had done to humanity.
Most English translations say Jesus was “deeply moved.”
But the Greek says:

“ἐνεβριμήσατο”
“Enebrimēsato.”
This word carries the idea of indignation, even anger.
The image is almost like a warhorse snorting before battle.
Jesus was not merely emotional.
He was confronting the enemy.
You knew.
Then they arrive at the tomb.
The Scripture says:
“It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.” — John 11:38
A cave.
A stone.
Burial imagery that foreshadows Christ’s own death.
John intentionally writes this connection.
Lazarus’ tomb points forward to another tomb.
But there is a crucial difference.
Lazarus would come out still wrapped in grave clothes.
Jesus would leave His behind forever.
Then Jesus commands:
“Take away the stone.”
Martha immediately protests:
“Lord, by this time there is a stench.” — John 11:39
The Greek phrase is brutally honest:
“ὄζει” (ozei)
“He smells.”
Decay had already begun.
Humanly speaking, Lazarus was beyond recovery.
And that is exactly where Jesus does His deepest work.
Some of you reading this have areas in your life you think are too far gone.
Too corrupted.
Too buried.
Too dead.
But Christ specializes in tombs everyone else gave up on.
Then Jesus prays publicly.
Not because He needs power from the Father.
But so the crowd would understand who He truly is.
And then the moment happens.
“Lazarus, come forth!” — John 11:43
In Greek:

“Λάζαρε, δεῦρο ἔξω!”
“Lazare, deuro exō!”
The early church fathers used to say that Jesus called Lazarus by name because if He had only shouted “Come forth,” every grave in Israel would have opened.
Because creation recognizes its Creator.
And death obeys His voice.
Immediately Lazarus emerges.
Bound hand and foot.
Alive, but still wrapped.
That matters.
Jesus then says:
“Loose him, and let him go.” — John 11:44
Salvation and sanctification appear together here.
Christ raises the dead.
Then the community helps remove the grave clothes.
Many people have received life from Christ but still walk wrapped in old identities, old addictions, old shame, old fears.
Alive spiritually.
But still bound.
But here’s the part rarely preached…
The resurrection of Lazarus directly triggered the final conspiracy to kill Jesus.
John 11:53 says:
“So from that day on they planned together to kill Him.”
Lazarus walking out of the tomb accelerated Jesus walking toward the Cross.
One resurrection led to another death.
At least temporarily.
Because Jesus did not raise Lazarus merely to comfort a grieving family.
He raised Lazarus to reveal what He Himself was about to accomplish permanently.
Lazarus came back to mortal life and would eventually die again.
Jesus rose into eternal glorified life, never to die again.
That is the Gospel.
Sin buried humanity in a tomb no human effort could escape.
Religion could not roll the stone away.
Morality could not resurrect the heart.
Good works could not conquer death.
But Jesus Christ entered the grave Himself.
The Hebrew prophet Isaiah foretold it centuries earlier:
“He was pierced for our transgressions…” — Isaiah 53:5
And three days after His crucifixion, the tomb could not hold Him.
This is why the Lazarus story matters.
It is not merely about one dead man in Bethany.
It is about every spiritually dead heart hearing the voice of Christ.
Ephesians 2:1 says:
“And you He made alive, who were dead in trespasses and sins.”
Dead.
Not sick.
Not struggling.
Dead.
Until Jesus called your name.
Maybe that is why this story unsettles people so deeply.
Because somewhere inside, you know there are chambers of your soul that smell like decay.
Hidden sin.
Secret compromise.
Bitterness.
Lust.
Pride.
Unforgiveness.
God saw it.
But the same Christ who stood before Lazarus’ tomb still calls dead things to life.
The question is whether you will stay in the grave.
Or respond when He calls your name.
There are people slowly drifting spiritually, convincing themselves they still have time. But conviction fades when ignored.
